title: 14. Chute exit velocity underrepresents true behavior and temperament compared with continuous accelerometer monitoring in feedlot steers.
content:
Abstract
Poor behavior and temperament of beef cattle have shown to negatively impact beef cattle production traits such as feed efficiency, thus reducing producer profitability in the long run. Cattle temperament has long been measured using subjective scores, or techniques that are less likely to reflect an animal’s true temperament and behavior over time. The objective of this study was to determine if accelerometer data is correlated with flight speed and feed efficiency data. Crossbred steers (n = 98) from a commercial ranch consisting of primarily commercial Angus x Simmental and minor Hereford or Red Angus genetics were managed in a feedlot setting as one contemporary group. Upon entering the feedlot, all steers were fitted with 701x Tpro tags to monitor steps and mounting behavior to obtain data on each animal for the duration of the study. Feed efficiency was collected via 12 Vytelle SENSETM feeders, over 147 days. Chute exit velocity was measured at three time points during the study, on day 0 (t1), mid-study (t2), and at the end of the study (t3), representing one of the common metrics used to characterize behavior. These data were analyzed in SAS v9.04 where the CORR procedure was utilized to generate Pearson correlations between variables of feed efficiency, chute exit velocity, mounting, and activity. Velocity at t1 was positively correlated (P < 0.0001) with Velocity at t2 (r = 0.47) and t3 (r = 0.61). None of the velocity metrics associated (P ≥ 0.13) with activity or mounting behavior determined by 701x Tpro tags. Velocity t1 and t2 positively associated (P ≤ 0.01) with ADG (r = 0.27 and 0.26, respectively). Activity was positively associated with mounting (P < 0.0001, r = 0.39) and negatively associated with ADG (P = 0.03, r= -0.21). Chute exit velocity, activity, and mounting measured by continuous monitoring are not correlated. This indicates that the traditional metric of chute velocity may be underrepresenting true activity and behavior. Interestingly, the inverse relationship between activity and ADG may indicate that animal behavior can influence performance and potential economic impact.
